title: Turkey stand-up comic released after being convicted of insulting Erdoğan
description: An Istanbul court has convicted a popular comedian of insulting President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan – and handed down a sentence of almost 19 months – but
body: An Istanbul court has convicted a popular comedian of insulting President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan – and handed down a sentence of almost 19 months – but ordered his release due to time served. It has also placed him under a travel ban, preventing him from travelling outside Turkey.A final decision in the case will come from the court of appeals.Deniz Göktaş - who denied the charges - has already spent nearly 90 days in prison. Prosecutors had asked for up to 12 years. His case comes amid a wave of arrests in Turkey that human rights groups say is aimed at crushing dissent.His stand-up routine went viral on YouTube, attracting more than 15 million views.Prosecutors had singled out a line in which the comedian called the Turkish leader "a shy dictator", but Göktaş insisted there was "no criminal element" in his comments. "Dictator is not an insult," he said, "it is a political characterisation."But angering the president in Turkey is not funny. Göktaş was arrested and handcuffed at Istanbul airport in July when he returned from a holiday.During his court appearance on Monday, it was clear he did not lose his sense of humour during his 88 days in solitary confinement."Three months have been taken away from my life," he said on the stand. "But I quit smoking, so I'll add another three months to my life." That drew laughter and loud applause in court.Outside, supporters like Firat Aksal – a fellow comedian – were very pleasantly surprised by the verdict.   "We hardly know what to do with our happiness," he said. "We are thrilled. To be honest we weren't hopeful of getting a fair trial. "Göktaş was released at 21:45 local time (18:45 GMT) and greeted by well-wishers, including his parents who he was seen hugging, outside a prison facility.Aksal said Göktaş would now rest for a few days, and see his family, and then return to the stage.After his release, Göktaş told reporters: "I'm very happy to be reunited with my family, mother, father, and friends."But he added: "There are thousands of other people in prisons across Turkey. Some, like me, are being held in pre-trial detention, while others have been convicted because of their views. "So, of course, it's wonderful to be out. I've missed it very much. But there is not much difference between inside and outside. I hope the day comes when we can all regain our freedom together."Many others remain behind bars, including journalists, human rights campaigners, student protesters, LGBTQ activists, and the elected Mayor of Istanbul, Ekrem Imamoglu. Prisons are full in Turkey these days.Erdogan and his party in the past have denied arrests, such as that of Imamoglu, have been politically motivated, insisting that Turkey's judiciary is independent.Additional reporting by Gunce Akpamuk

schema.headline: Turkey stand-up comic released after being convicted of insulting Erdoğan

title: Plan for controversial Sydney data centre scrapped after push-back
description: Plans for a data centre which would have been built metres from people's homes in a Sydney suburb have been scrapped following intense push-back by ca
body: Plans for a data centre which would have been built metres from people's homes in a Sydney suburb have been scrapped following intense push-back by campaigners. The data centre was being developed by Goodman Group, Australia's biggest property company, and would have seen it construct a A$1.2bn (£630m; $841m), 90-megawatt facility known as Project Mars in the Lane Cove area.The company confirmed it was withdrawing its application in a letter to the local planning authority. It follows a concerted opposition against the data centre by local residents and campaigners. The dispute captures a wider disagreement in Australia over the role of data centres. With the mainstreaming of generative AI in recent years, there has been a huge swell in demand for data centres, and Australia - with its abundance of clean energy, natural gas reserves, and land - has become a global destination for their construction. However, while the country's government has been keen to attract investment from global AI companies, there has also been stiff opposition due to the huge demands the centres place on water and energy supplies, and the disruption they cause local communities. The proposal for Project Mars, which would have been constructed about 20 metres from the nearest house in the suburb of Lane Cove, received 374 submissions during a consultation - with just nine in support of it. According to local news website In the Cove, this is highest number of submissions ever received for a data centre application, external. In its letter to New South Wales Department of Planning, Goodman Group said since starting the planning process in March 2025, it had "undertaken extensive technical investigations, stakeholder engagement and community consultation". "During this time, the policy and regulatory environment for large-scale data centre development has evolved significantly," it said. It said it had "carefully considered these changes" along with the "views of the local community", and concluded it would not proceed with the development.The decision by Goodman Group follows an announcement by the New South Wales government last month that it would be introducing a fast-track programme for data centres. The programme would allow them to be assessed within 75 days, provided they meet requirements around certain standards and fund the additional supply of water and energy. In a message posted to the Facebook page of Lane Cove Responsible Planning Group, Anthony Roberts, a member of the New South Wales Legislative Assembly representing Lane Cove, said it was "a huge win for the Lane Cove West community". "This is a common-sense win for our community," he said. "This victory sends a clear message to other data centre developers. To find suitable locations before putting proposals forward."Data centres have an important role to play, but developments of this size and scale need to be appropriately located and planned with the surrounding community in mind."

schema.headline: Plan for controversial Sydney data centre scrapped after push-back

title: German town bans stumbling stone memorials to Nazi victims
description: There has been a wave of criticism in Germany after the town of Heidenau, near Dresden in Saxony, decided to ban "stumbling stone" memorials to victim
body: There has been a wave of criticism in Germany after the town of Heidenau, near Dresden in Saxony, decided to ban "stumbling stone" memorials to victims of the Nazis.Germany's Education Minister Karin Prien told newspaper Bild that the ban was a "scandal".Since the 1990s, many towns in countries across Europe, including in Germany and Austria, have embedded small brass plaques in the streets in memory of Jews and other victims of Nazi atrocities.The plaques, called Stolpersteine in German, are often placed outside the houses where the victims used to live or work. They are frequently funded by donations.But now councillors from the Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) party and the conservative CDU in Heidenau have voted to ban stumbling stones in their town.The AfD in Saxony has been classified as extreme-right by German intelligence, a designation the party rejects.The motion in the town council said that many citizens felt that this form of commemoration of Nazi victims was inappropriate. Memorials should in future be placed at the city's Nordfriedhof cemetery to make it "impossible to step directly onto the memorial elements", the motion stated.However, Karin Prien, a member of the CDU, criticised the decision."Anyone who banishes Stolpersteine and memorial sites commemorating Jewish life from public spaces to the cemetery is prioritising death over life and rendering Jewish people invisible once again," she told Bild.She said her own CDU party in Saxony also bore responsibility for the decision.Charlotte Knobloch, a Holocaust survivor and president of the Jewish Community in Munich, said that removing memorials from the cityscape was "completely the wrong approach".She told the Funke Media Group that she was "appalled that a democratic party would stoop to supporting such a transparent manoeuvre by the extremists of the AfD".Knobloch said that she was not a supporter of the stumbling stones, but added that "decentralised remembrance – which is not banished from public space but, on the contrary, permeates and shapes it" was crucial to a genuine culture of remembrance.In her own city of Munich, there are no Stolpersteine on municipal land. Instead, the city allows memorial plaques on public buildings.As the name suggests, Stolpersteine are intended as memorials people stumble upon, making them reflect on the history of their location.Gunter Demnig, the artist who initiated the Stolperstein project, said that given the recent electoral successes of the AfD "it was certainly to be expected that something like this would happen".The AfD recently secured major victories in state elections in Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Vorpommern.Some branches of the populist AfD are classed as right-wing extremist by domestic intelligence, a designation the party strongly rejects.Its anti-immigration, "Germany first" and Russian-friendly agenda has found fertile ground in the country's former communist east.

schema.headline: German town bans stumbling stone memorials to Nazi victims

title: Nigeria's Ben Dancer attempts to break world record for non-stop dancing
description: A Nigerian dancer is attempting to dance non-stop for seven days in order to set a new world record.Benjamin Daniel, known as Ben Dancer, is aiming to
body: A Nigerian dancer is attempting to dance non-stop for seven days in order to set a new world record.Benjamin Daniel, known as Ben Dancer, is aiming to dance for 168 hours - 41 hours longer than the current record for the longest individual dance marathon.Guinness World Records has yet to confirm whether the attempt qualifies as an official record. The BBC has contacted the organisation for comment.Young people have been gathering in recent days to cheer him on at Freedom Park in Lagos, filming his every move and dancing along from behind the barriers."It's a beautiful moment. Seeing how far he has come and witnessing him achieve this feat made me incredibly proud and grateful to God," Uche Anumudu, one of those watching, told the BBC.The current record is 127 hours, set by Indian dancer Srushti Sudhir Jagtap in 2023, when she was 16. Her performance focused mainly on kathak, one of India's major classical dance forms.Ben Dancer, 33, has been dancing professionally for 18 years.His attempt began on Tuesday 22 September and, if he completes the planned 168 hours, he is due to reach his target early on Tuesday morning.For much of the marathon, Ben Dancer has drawn on Nigeria's rich dance traditions as well as its fast-changing internet culture.Afrobeats has been a constant presence, alongside genres including fuji,  jazz and zouk.The scene around him has become something of a street party. Crowds of young people have gathered to cheer him on. Videos from the attempt have gone viral across social media platforms, drawing more people to the venue.Moronumubo Akodu, who has repeatedly visited to support Ben Dancer, said she was impressed by his determination but worried about the physical toll."It is actually insane but I am so proud of him," she told the BBC.Emmanuel Ulelu, who visited the performance twice, said he noticed a striking change in the dancer's energy."On day two, you could see the stress," he said. "Even after just three hours of dancing at the location myself, I wondered how he would keep going."But when he returned 16 hours into day five, he said Ben Dancer appeared more energetic than before."It reminded me that we're capable of doing unbelievable things when how badly we want something matches and surpasses the difficulty of achieving it," he said.Nigeria has also developed a strong relationship with Guinness World Records, particularly in entertainment.In 2023, Nigerian chef Hilda Baci cooked continuously for 93 hours and 11 minutes in Lagos, which Guinness officially recognised as a new record.Her achievement sparked a surge of interest in record attempts in Nigeria, even though others have since surpassed her.Guinness says it received more than 1,500 new applications from the country within two months of her cook-a-thon, including events such as reading, singing, and crocheting.

schema.headline: Nigeria's Ben Dancer attempts to break world record for non-stop dancing

title: Embattled Serbian president resigns, paving way for early elections
description: Serbia's president has resigned after more than a year of student-led protests and growing public discontent over allegations of government corruption
body: Serbia's president has resigned after more than a year of student-led protests and growing public discontent over allegations of government corruption.Aleksandar Vučić said his administration had preserved peace and stability during his nine-year tenure as he addressed supporters outside the presidential building in the capital, Belgrade.He had already announced his intention to resign in June and is currently standing to be his party's candidate for prime minister in the upcoming parliamentary elections. Vučić cannot run for a third presidential term under Serbia's constitution.The populist leader's administration has been dogged by anger over alleged corner-cutting.It was the collapse of the Novi Sad railway station's roof, killing 16 people, that first galvanised anger towards the government in 2024.Protests involving a wide range of citizens - from students and teachers to workers and farmers - followed.Demonstrators believed that the disaster reflected more than a decade of governing by the Progressive Party of Vucic, who closely associated himself with the station's renovation, which was supposed to be a symbol of Serbia's progress.A series of resignations of those under the embattled president failed to placate the protesters, who continued to demonstrate throughout this summer, turning to unrest following accusations of police brutality.Vučić's presidency was due to expire next year. Under Serbia's constitution, presidential elections must be held no more than three months after his resignation.This means Serbians will go to the polls twice before the end of the year.Vučić said the presidential election will take place more than a month after the snap parliamentary election in late October, itself called in response to the protests, which had added calls for a vote to their list of demands.He had earlier announced that he planned to run in that election as Progressive Party's leader, leaving the possibility he could retain a position at the top of Serbian politics.Parliamentary speaker Ana Brnabić, also a Progressive Party member, will assume the role of interim president until a new one is elected.Vučić used his constitutional powers to pardon 49 people, including 23 students and party loyalists suspected of offences related to what he called the "terrible events we have gone through over the past year and a half", according to Serbian public broadcaster RTS.The upcoming parliamentary elections will pit Vučić's Progressive Party against a student-led, anti-corruption movement called Students Win and a coalition of pro-Western opposition parties known as European Serbia.Vucic has been a fixture of Serbian politics for more than a decade, becoming prime minister in 2014, before being elected to his first term as president in 2017.He has publicly said he wants Serbia to join the EU while courting close ties with Russia and opening Serbia up to Chinese investment.

schema.headline: Embattled Serbian president resigns, paving way for early elections

title: Trump-Xi summit: What wasn't said might matter the most
description: Chinese state media confirmed for the first time on Monday that the trade truce has been extended until 10 January.The short extension ensures both le
body: Chinese state media confirmed for the first time on Monday that the trade truce has been extended until 10 January.The short extension ensures both leaders will meet again at major international gatherings later this year.Trump will attend the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen in November while Xi is due to travel to Miami for the G20 summit in December.It is rare for the leaders of the world's two largest economies to meet so frequently.But Beijing had hoped for a much longer extension to the truce, making the two month reprieve a modest gain rather than a major breakthrough.China did secure lower tariffs on $30bn (£23bn) of goods entering the US with reciprocal reductions expected from Beijing.Chinese products heading to American stores ranging from toys to small household appliances to Christmas decorations will benefit from the lower tariffs.The Trump administration also said Beijing would buy at least 10 million metric tons of coal annually in 2027 and 2028.What is striking is what was left out.There was no mention of increasing exports of China's rare earth minerals to the US nor was there any indication that restrictions on advanced US semiconductors would be eased.The White House factsheet made no mention of Taiwan, but the issue was clearly a priority for Xi Jinping.According to Beijing's accounts of the talks, Xi urged Donald Trump to formally oppose Taiwan independence and handle the issue with caution.After their previous meeting in May, Trump revealed that Xi directly asked him if the US would defend Taiwan in the event of a Chinese attack.He told reporters, "There's only one person that knows that, and it is me," and he raised the question whether it made sense for US forces to "travel 9,500 miles to fight a war" over the issue.This time, Trump disclosed far less."We didn't talk about it too much," he told reporters over the weekend."Right now, it's fine. It's just moving along," Trump said. "He understands very much how I feel."That silence may be significant.Trump has previously described a proposed $14bn US arms package for Taiwan as "a very good negotiating chip" in his dealings with Beijing. The arms package has been on hold for months.Adding to the confusion, US Ambassador to China David Perdue told Fox News that Trump had offered to sell weapons to Xi during the summit.The State Department later clarified that US law prohibits arms sales to China and there are no plans to do so.Beijing sees the self-governing island as part of China. Most countries, including the United States, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.China says it will allow more foreign financial firms, including American-backed banks, investment companies and insurers, to apply to do business and open offices in China. But any approvals will still be subject to Chinese laws and regulations.The last line is key. China is opening the door, but still controls who gets through it.Foreign financial firms have long complained that regulatory barriers, licensing requirements and concerns over exit bans make it difficult to expand in China, even when market access is technically allowed.Beijing also said it was discussing ways to increase the number of flights between both countries, but neither side has explained how this would happen.And despite giving visa free entry to visitors from more than 75 countries across the world, China has not extended that offer to Americans.Meanwhile the US State Department continues to classify travel to China as a Level 2 advisory urging travellers to "exercise increased caution" because of the risk of arbitrary law enforcement, exit bans and detention.So even though both sides are talking about encouraging business and travel some of the biggest obstacles remain firmly in place.

schema.headline: Trump-Xi summit: What wasn't said might matter the most

title: News media must stay relevant or 'society will struggle', says World News Day organiser
description: World News Day has grown since it began in 2018, and its message that "trusted journalism matters" aims to highlight the role of news providers in inv
body: World News Day has grown since it began in 2018, and its message that "trusted journalism matters" aims to highlight the role of news providers in investigating and explaining important events.It comes against a backdrop of what the recent Reuters Institute report described as "anxiety, disengagement, and cynicism" towards news among the public, "but also openness to new sources and formats, and continued belief in what news at its best can offer".Social media and video networks overtook news organisations' own websites and apps as the main source of online news last year, but are trusted less, the report said.In another report, published earlier this month, UK media regulator Ofcom, external also said people now get news from a wider variety of sources, with YouTube "growing rapidly" and 20% of people using AI tools to access news.But growing choice has gone hand-in-hand with greater uncertainty about who and what to believe, and traditional providers are still seen as more trustworthy, accurate and impartial than online platforms, Ofcom said.Brkic, who founded South Africa's Daily Maverick, accepts that the media landscape has changed, and said established news organisations must respond."The old days are not coming back. We need to form a new equilibrium, and the only way we can do it is that if we actually join forces," he said."If we continue like this, we're just going to be weak individual players waiting to be taken out. If we don't change something pretty fundamentally and pretty urgently, we're just going to be roadkill."Brkic said the mainstream media has "committed mistakes", but professional and reliable journalists play a vital role in society."We need to talk to our audiences and explain to them, it's not in your interest not to choose truth and trust," he said."We cannot function without a thing called the truth, without facts."The definition of "the truth" is often contested, however, as seen in US President Donald Trump's long-running battle with what he labels the "fake news media".Brkic added: "This is the information-based society. We are the infrastructure for that information-based society. And that society is actually going to really struggle without us."

schema.headline: News media must stay relevant or 'society will struggle', says World News Day organiser

title: Ekurhuleni killings: What we know after bodies of 12 women found in South Africa
description: Case 12Boitumelo Gift Mashita was shot and killed on Monday in Tembisa Ekurhuleni. The 23-year-old woman was on her way to work when she was gunned do
body: Case 12Boitumelo Gift Mashita was shot and killed on Monday in Tembisa Ekurhuleni. The 23-year-old woman was on her way to work when she was gunned down and her belongings were taken. Police say her estranged husband, who they suspected of being responsible for her murder, was later found dead inside his vehicle in Midrand.Police have not found any link between this case and the discovery of the other bodies.While most of the bodies were found in the same area, police confirmed the discovery of another body about 39 miles (63 km) away from Ekurhuleni on 20 September. The body of a young woman, believed to be in her 20s, was found wrapped in a duvet in a dam in Soweto, south-west of Johannesburg. It's unclear if her murder is linked to those in Ekurhuleni.President Cyril Ramaphosa said the killing of these women and others was a "stain on our national conscience".South Africa has one of the highest homicide rates, with 5,427 people murdered between April and June this year alone.South African police statistics do not differentiate victims by gender but the South African Human Rights Commission said last week that 569 women were killed between April and June this year. This works out as an average of six women killed each day.Police have set up a task team to investigate these murders and have offered a reward of 400,000 rand ($24,000; £18,000) for information that could lead to arrests.

schema.headline: Ekurhuleni killings: What we know after bodies of 12 women found in South Africa

title: Time running out for Tennessee killer Christa Pike who says she's too damaged for death row
description: Killer Christa Pike to be executed within days - but her defence say she's a victim tooImage source, Tennesse Department of CorrectionsImage caption,
body: Killer Christa Pike to be executed within days - but her defence say she's a victim tooImage source, Tennesse Department of CorrectionsImage caption, Christa Pike's lawyers have filed a clemency petition seeking to commute her sentence ahead of the 30 September execution date ByStephanie HegartyBBC World Service correspondentAshlee Sellars last heard from her friend Christa Pike earlier this week, when Pike texted her from her cell on death row as she prepares to be killed by lethal injection by the US state of Tennessee.Pike told Sellars she did not want any of her loved ones to be present on Wednesday when she is executed. "She doesn't want us to experience that," Sellars says.Sellars finds it hard to reconcile this woman, whom she has only known to be kind and protective, with the person who committed a heinous crime 31 years ago.Pike, now 50, was 18 when she and her boyfriend at the time, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and murdered Colleen Slemmer, a 19-year-old they met at a job training camp for troubled teens.The murder created a media frenzy in Knoxville, Tennessee in 1995, when Colleen was found with a pentagram - a symbol of Satanic ritual - carved into her chest.Pike had accused Colleen of insulting her and trying to steal her boyfriend. Two other residents at the camp later testified that Pike had bragged about the murder before and after, and showed them a piece of Colleen's skull.A year later she was sentenced to death, while Shipp - who was 17 at the time - was given a life sentence with the possibility of parole. Now, after years of failed appeals, Pike's execution has been set. If it goes ahead, she will be the first woman put to death in Tennessee in more than 200 years. Only 18 women have been executed in the US since the 1970s, compared to 1,663 men.Colleen's mother has said she wants Pike's execution to happen so that her daughter "finally can be resting".Image source, Family handoutImage caption, Student Colleen Slemmer was tortured and brutally killed in the 1995 murderBut Pike's lawyers, who filed a 226-page clemency petition, are still hoping for a last-minute reprieve, while UN human rights experts have also called for the execution to be stopped., external Pike has a documented history of childhood sexual abuse, abandonment and neglect. Her lawyers believe that if she was found guilty of the same crime today as a teenager she would not receive a death sentence.In the years since her sentencing, her defence team have uncovered details about her childhood that they say the jury never had the chance to consider."It is mind-boggling that they did not present any of her history of abuse and rape, even though they knew about it," says Sandra Babcock, an expert in gender and the death penalty at Cornell Law School, who has worked on Pike's defence."Her case is so uniquely compelling, not just because of her really incomprehensible history of sexual violence but the combination of that with her youth and her mental illness."Image source, Christa PikeImage caption, Christa Pike suffered neglect and was abused by her parentsIn 1995, forensic psychologist Dr Diana McCoy was hired by Pike's defence team and found she was severely neglected by both of her parents. McCoy's report found Pike was physically and sexually abused by several of her mother's husbands and boyfriends, and raped several times, once when she was 11 and again aged 17. Later, it was discovered that she was repeatedly raped as a toddler by her grandmother's boyfriend. McCoy said Pike's mother didn't believe her that these rapes happened.But Pike's trial lawyer did not put McCoy on the stand or call many of the witnesses she recommended. These details emerged over a decade later in a court hearing reviewing her case, when a new team of lawyers claimed ineffective assistance of counsel, a claim that was denied by the judge.In 2021, Pike was diagnosed with bipolar disorder in prison and has been medicated since.Later, another forensic psychologist working for Pike's defence, Dr Bethany Brand, who assessed Pike in 2023, said her case was extremely rare because she was abused by so many people who should have protected her."Her childhood was replete with physical, sexual and emotional abuse. She was sexually violated by a number of men, starting before she was school age," she says.Brand says Pike had untreated manic episodes due to bipolar disorder and untreated PTSD. "Both of those things together absolutely influenced how threatened she felt by the girl she ended up killing and her lack of emotional control in that situation."Babcock adds: "If they let her be executed, then what it tells us is that the death penalty in this country is just a joke. It's not for the worst of the worst. It is for the people who receive the worst legal representation and who are the most damaged and vulnerable."Image source, Christa PikeImage caption, Pike, pictured as a teenager, killed Slemmer in January 1995 after telling a friend she "just felt mean that day", court documents say'She should pay for it'Last year, Tennessee's Supreme Court ruled Pike had not shown circumstances that would justify commuting her sentence. Her appeals process had been exhausted and a date was set for her execution.A federal appeals court had earlier ruled that the jury had already heard about her difficult childhood during testimony from her mother, father and aunt during her trial. And that new evidence of bipolar disorder, PTSD and brain damage "mostly repeated" what the jury had heard and would not have changed the verdict. The row has some parallels with the high-profile case of murderer Lisa Montgomery, whose lawyers also argued she was a mentally ill victim of abuse who deserved mercy.Montgomery's legal challenges failed to commute her sentence and she was executed by lethal injection in Indiana in 2021.Unless she is granted clemency by Tennessee Governor Bill Lee, Pike will be executed on 30 September. That decision is unlikely to come until the last moment and Lee has never before granted clemency in a death penalty case.The Tennessee Supreme Court this week denied Pike's request to halt the execution. Her counsel say they have been discussing next steps.On her execution day, Pike has requested an all-female team. She says being held down by a group of men will exacerbate her trauma. The state of Tennessee has said the goal is that female guards will transfer Pike to the prison where she will be executed but hasn't guaranteed it.Colleen's mother May Martinez supports Christa's execution."She did the crime. I think she should pay for it," she said on Knoxville TV station WBIR in 2021, and told the BBC this week she still stands by those comments.Pike should suffer before she dies, Martinez told WBIR. "I would feel better that she felt the same pain that Colleen did."Image source, J. Miles Carey/USA TODAY/Imagn Images via ReutersImage caption, May Martinez, mother of Colleen Slemmer, and a retired Knoxville Police department detective outside a courtroom for a post-conviction hearing in 2006"My heart breaks every single day because I keep reliving it and reliving it, and I can't no more, and I want this to happen before I die," she added."There's not a day goes by that I don't think about Colleen or how she died and how rough it was. I just want Christa down so I can end it, relieve my daughter, so she finally can be resting."The Justice Coalition, a victims' rights advocacy group, has raised money to help Martinez travel to Tennessee to watch the execution.The group's executive director, Robert Bracewell, said this sentence was determined by a jury of Pike's peers and it was what Colleen's family want."We stand firm with the family that on the 30 September her execution ought to proceed."Ashlee Sellars grapples with two seemingly conflicting beliefs: that Colleen's mother has a right to feel justice has been served and that everyone, including her friend Christa, deserves a chance at redemption."When I think about reconciling who you see on TV or the horrible tragedy that happened with Colleen, the only thing that makes sense to me is around mental health and trauma and the way that people process stuff in a moment when they don't have the things that they need," Sellars says."These horrible things happen in your youth and then those traumas moved through you, in our community, and you cause harm to somebody else."Sellars met Pike in prison while serving a 25-year sentence for her involvement in a robbery-murder. They spoke to each other through the meal flaps in their doors on the high security unit. Now, Sellars works as an advocate for justice reform and victims of crime."People want to know that everyone's life matters, right? They want to know that Colleen's life mattered," she says."Christa in this moment, I think she is fighting much more for her life to matter than she is to actually live."

schema.headline: Time running out for Tennessee killer Christa Pike who says she's too damaged for death row

title: Before BTS and Blackpink, there was Big Bang: Now the 'Kings of K-pop' are back
description: Image source, Timothy Norris/Getty ImagesImage caption, Taeyang, G-Dragon and Daesung of BigBang perform during the 2026 Coachella Valley Music and Ar
body: Image source, Timothy Norris/Getty ImagesImage caption, Taeyang, G-Dragon and Daesung of BigBang perform during the 2026 Coachella Valley Music and Arts FestivalByJiji Ahn A sea of glowing yellow crowns. Thousands of voices chanting in Korean.An explosive surge of energy as the opening synth riffs of Fantastic Baby shatter the stadium air. Big Bang is back.Fourteen years after their first major European shows, and after a decade marked by military service, member departures and legal scandals, the South Korean group played at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium in London on Saturday as part of their 20th anniversary world tour.Inside the near-capacity venue, the crowd did not just watch a concert - they stepped into a significant moment in K-pop history.As the band emerged in their trademark high-fashion, glittering outfits, the crowd danced freely, setting the tone for an evening that felt less like a routine tour stop and more like a homecoming.Image caption, Inside Tottenham Hotspur StadiumFor fans, it is a long-awaited reunion. But the significance of Big Bang's return extends beyond nostalgia.Years before BTS were selling out Wembley Stadium and Blackpink were headlining Hyde Park, Big Bang were already proving Korean pop could succeed far beyond Asia.The group filled arenas across the West, collaborated with major American artists, experimented with hip-hop and electronic music, and turned their own fashion and creative identities into part of their appeal.Having attended their European debut at Wembley Arena in 2012, the shift in atmosphere on Saturday was striking.Where their original UK shows were driven by a hunger to prove themselves and promote a new album, this return as a trio, comprising G-Dragon, Taeyang and Daesung, felt entirely crafted for their dedicated community. By reworking classic tracks and cleverly remixing songs to accommodate absent members, the group relied on pyrotechnics, their signature live band and sheer stage presence rather than elaborate staging.The result was a reunion that felt celebratory, grounded and playful.Image source, YG EntertainmentImage caption, G-Dragon, Taeyang and Daesung on stage with dancersIn 2011, Big Bang became the first K-pop group to win a major Western music award when they took home the newly created Worldwide Act prize at the MTV Europe Music Awards.When they made their European debut at Wembley Arena in December 2012, a second show was added after the first sold out in under two hours.They were leading a pioneering generation that proved global crossover was genuinely possible. Then in 2016, Forbes estimated Big Bang had earned $44m (£33.2m) over the previous year, making them the first K-pop act to appear on its Celebrity 100 List."When it comes to the global market for K-pop, there is no doubt Big Bang made a huge contribution," says Dr Haekyung Um, senior lecturer in music at the University of Liverpool."Earlier acts were popular within Asian markets, but Big Bang were true international stars. I would call them the Kings of K-pop, just as we call Michael Jackson the King of Pop," Um adds."Big Bang's success really was an early signal of how successful a K-pop stadium tour in the West could truly be."Image source, YG EntertainmentImage caption, G-Dragon, Taeyang, and Daesung celebrating their 20th anniversary during the XX: Cosmos World TourBefore Big Bang, K-pop groups were often viewed as heavily manufactured by entertainment agencies.But music critics say Big Bang broke the mould. They wrote and produced their own songs, shaped their own streetwear image and blended genres ranging from hip-hop and R&B to trot, a traditional South Korean folk genre.For many attending on Saturday, the show served as a direct lesson in K-pop's lineage - a chance to see "the idols' idols" perform live."They were different because they didn't follow the uniform K-pop cookie-cutter pretty boy phase," explains Sharon, who was visiting London from Singapore. "They went harder on their music, a bit more hip-hop. They did what they had to do, and they are the absolute OGs for me."The shift set them apart across Asia and helped establish the blueprint for modern self-produced acts such as BTS.Image caption, Fans arrived kitted out with Big Bang merchandise And then there is the yellow crown. At Big Bang concerts, it is impossible to miss the group's crown-shaped lightstick, known as the Bang Bong.In early K-pop, fans supported artists by waving coloured balloons or generic glow sticks.But seeking a distinct, permanent identity for their fandom, dubbed "VIPs", band leader G-Dragon proposed a handheld yellow crown, setting the template for custom concert merchandise."Fan engagement and coordinated chants have deep roots in Korean music history," explains Um. "But Big Bang helped modernise the physical technology."The Bang Bong established a model for custom-designed fandom lightsticks and merchandise that modern K-pop groups now follow. Outside the venue, that same fan-led energy spilled into the streets, with attendees trading handmade gifts and photo cards - a ritual that has spread to Western arena tours in recent years. Volunteer fan groups distributed roughly 35,000 custom-printed banners across the stadium, co-ordinating a massive crowd-wide salute to be raised in unison during select performances.Image caption, Fans exchanging handmade gifts outside the stadium Big Bang's story, however, is far from a straightforward tale of success. South Korea requires able-bodied men to complete mandatory military service, and Big Bang's members served at different points during the group's hiatus.Then came the scandals.In 2017, former band member T.O.P was convicted of marijuana use, an offence heavily criminalised and socially taboo in South Korea, and received a suspended prison sentence while serving his mandatory military duty. He later formally departed from the group.Then in 2019, the group's youngest member, Seungri, permanently retired from entertainment amid the "Burning Sun" scandal. It was a high-profile police investigation into a Seoul nightclub of the same name which exposed a network of sex trafficking, bribery, and illicit filming involving several male K-pop stars.South Korea's Supreme Court later upheld an 18-month prison sentence for Seungri in 2022 on charges including prostitution mediation, overseas gambling, and embezzlement.Image caption, Fans with their merchandise, holding up free banners ahead of the showAlthough the band didn't openly acknowledge the departure of two of their former members from the stage, their absence was obvious to long-time fans in the audience.Though it did not matter to fans like Annie, who flew from New York to see the show with friends. She said Big Bang's perseverance through hardship made their music mean even more."Big Bang was my starter," she says. "I love how they move through the obstacles - it gives me hope. After years of hiatus, it's amazing they're coming back. They are the OGs."The crowd erupted as the opening chant of Bang Bang Bang echoed before the band even walked out, while their iconic 2008 ballad Haru Haru produced a massive stadium-wide singalong.Image caption, Fans meeting up ahead of the concertThe K-pop industry Big Bang helped build has changed almost beyond recognition.Yet their return has drawn a striking mix of original second-generation fans and younger Gen Z listeners who were barely born when the group debuted.While many veteran followers grew up alongside the band, a whole new generation discovered them through digital archives or cross-media appearances. Gemma and her daughter Casey travelled from Edinburgh wearing handmade custom jackets. "I found out about them through T.O.P in Squid Game and then fell down a rabbit hole," Gemma says. "I've converted so many of my friends to K-pop now. It's all about the energy."For Korean diaspora fans, the show carried an even deeper cultural resonance. "I got into Big Bang when their Alive EP (in 2012) was released because I felt they were quite ground-breaking," says Kevin. "Before, I felt there was a lot of mimicking by Korean artists on what was happening in the West, but here they took full ownership of their unique identity. It's very rare in K-pop that you have a band around for 20 years, and they definitely played a part in making K-pop mainstream."Image caption, Nicole and her son Arthur attended the concert to celebrate his 8th birthday Much of this multi-generational pull is driven by archival concert footage, TV appearances, and classic music videos circulating across social media platforms like TikTok and YouTube."Nostalgia can be built upon something people didn't even experience personally at the time," notes Um. "It comes through shared digital memory. YG Entertainment was early in leveraging digital platforms like YouTube, which built a lasting global fan foundation that has accumulated across two generations."While the band refrained from directly addressing their past on stage, the emotional weight of their history peaked during the finale Still Life. As T.O.P's unmistakable baritone echoed through the stadium via recorded vocals, a visible wave of emotion swept across the crowd.Addressing the venue during the encore, G-Dragon appeared clearly moved, admitting they never expected their music to leave such an enduring global mark 14 years after their London debut.As fireworks lit up the night sky, the three members linked hands and bowed deeply - a triumphant moment for the group widely credited with helping reshape modern K-pop.

schema.headline: Before BTS and Blackpink, there was Big Bang: Now the 'Kings of K-pop' are back

title: French PM Lecornu warns against escalation of school protests
description: France's Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has warned that any escalation in the country's current wave of student protests would be "irresponsible", f
body: France's Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has warned that any escalation in the country's current wave of student protests would be "irresponsible", following the arrests of 164 people on Monday. The demonstrations, which began in Paris and have seen teenagers blockading their schools for days, stem from issues including overcrowded classes and teacher shortages. Lecornu cited reported incidents at protests in a post on X, saying: "Fireworks, fires, violence near high schools: nothing justifies endangering students, staff, or police officers."But a French union that defends the interests of high school students said the protests were a "legitimate response" to the conditions they face.Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said 12 members of the security forces, 12 students and three school staff were injured on Monday, while 180 schools were affected.He did not provide further details on those who had been arrested. The movement at French lycées, equivalent to sixth form in the UK or high school in the US, began last week in the Île-de-France region around Paris.Incidents of vandalism were reported, along with fireworks being aimed at police,  and the protests have now spread to other regions in France. According to the AFP news agency, four high schools were reported to have been blockaded in the southern regions of Alpes-Maritimes and Var. Protests have also been reported in Marseille, the northern Lille area and Sedan in the north-eastern Ardennes.The Union Syndicale Lycéenne, which represents students, defended the protests in a post on social media. "Lack of teachers and staff, dilapidated schools, overcrowded schedules and classes, stress caused by Parcoursup [the web platform used in France for students to apply to the first year of higher education]... These issues are by no means inevitable, but simply the result of 10 years of Macron's policies and the lack of resources in the national education system," it said.It called on students to blockade schools on Tuesday in defence of "their rights and against budget austerity".On the same day, unions representing teachers, hospital staff and civil servants also called for a day of walkouts to protest against issues including low wages and working conditions.In response to the student movement, Lecornu said "the difficulties of high schools must be heard and addressed", but that "violence must be condemned unequivocally, and its perpetrators must answer for their actions".The prime minister also accused the far-left France Unbowed (LFI) party of urging students to expand the movement.Jean-Luc Mélenchon, LFI's leader, blamed the Lecornu government for having "ordered the crackdown" on the protest, adding that the high school students taking part were "harmless".But Nuñez said the demonstrations and blockades were "not very typical protest movements"."It is much more like urban violence, with a number of individuals who were masked, equipped with fireworks in tubes, equipped with projectiles, who clearly wanted to confront the internal security forces," he said."It wasn't about making demands; it was really violence in its purest form."Since the protests began, several incidents involving violence between students and police officers have been reported.In one incident, a police officer reportedly fired a round from a grenade launcher used for crowd control, injuring a high school student, according to France's BFMTV.Investigations have been launched into these incidents, the broadcaster added.

schema.headline: French PM Lecornu warns against escalation of school protests

title: One dead as nor'easter storm pummels New York and New Jersey
description: Figure caption, Watch: Huge waves pummel northeast US as storm barrels throughByKwasi Gyamfi AsieduUpdated 28 September 2026Tens of millions of people
body: Figure caption, Watch: Huge waves pummel northeast US as storm barrels throughByKwasi Gyamfi AsieduUpdated 28 September 2026Tens of millions of people across the north-eastern US have found themselves in the path of a powerful weekend storm bringing coastal flooding, power cuts, travel chaos and cancelled stadium events.The so-called nor'easter brought "dangerous coastal flooding and beach conditions, strong winds and heavy rainfall" to areas including New York City and Boston on Saturday, the US National Weather Service (NWS) said. States of emergency have been declared in New York and New Jersey, both of which faced a coastal deluge in some areas. Rain and strong winds were forecast from Virginia to Maine.In Brooklyn, New York City, a man was killed by a falling tree.Figure caption, BBC Weather presenter Helen Willetts look at the impacts of the powerful Nor'easterThe man has been identified as 56-year-old Leighton Brown, an employee of the New York City Housing Authority.According to local news, he was walking through east Brooklyn neighbourhood working an extra shift when the deadly incident occurred."We mourn deeply for the loss of Leighton Brown, a NYCHA employee who faithfully served Brooklyn residents and who was known for his warm personality," the Office of the NYC Public Advocate wrote on social media.The nor'easter has caused widespread power cuts. More than 160,000 households, nearly all in the north-eastern US, have lost electricity, according to tracker PowerOutage. More than 2,400 flights were delayed and another 1,199 grounded on Saturday, according to FlightAware.A full moon was projected to worsen coastal flooding. Streets and homes were inundated with floodwater in the coastal New Jersey communities of Surf City and Manasquan on Saturday.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Surf City, New Jersey, was among coastal communities floodedNWS said in its alert: "Prepare immediately for significant inundation in low-lying areas near the shore, including roads underwater and impacts to homes and businesses." In New York, officials are warning of wind gusts of up to 55mph (86km/h) throughout the weekend, leading to downed trees and power lines."Don't travel if you don't have to," NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani told residents in a video message. "Do not drive or walk through floodwater."In the Boston area, the Red Sox moved the last game in their series against the Chicago Cubs to Sunday afternoon in Florida. Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Residents on kayaks in a Beach Haven West, New Jersey, neighbourhoodA professional football match between Red Bull New York and St Louis City SC was also cancelled. The Global Citizen Festival concert in New York City's Central Park, which was to be headlined by Lauryn Hill, Wyclef Jean and John Legend, will not go ahead.Ed Sheeran's Boston concert was also among events called off due to the weather.Sheeran's concert at the Gillette Stadium in the Boston area was cancelled for safety reasons, the venue said.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Streets and homes were inundated with floodwater in coastal parts of New JerseyImage source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Waves pounded the coast in Massachusetts

schema.headline: One dead as nor'easter storm pummels New York and New Jersey

title: Hurricane Polo unleashes threatening winds as it approaches Mexico
description: Hurricane Polo is lashing the northern Pacific coast of Mexico with intense winds as it moves ashore with the threat of life-threatening flash floods.
body: Hurricane Polo is lashing the northern Pacific coast of Mexico with intense winds as it moves ashore with the threat of life-threatening flash floods. The powerful category three storm, with maximum sustained winds near 115 mph (185 km/h), is expected to make landfall on Monday evening over the state of Baja California Sur, a region popular with tourists and home to the resort destination of Los Cabos.Meteorologists at the US-based National Hurricane Center (NHC) have warned that life-threatening winds and flash foods had begun to hit portions of the regionResidents boarded up homes and businesses and stocked up on essentials such as drinking water and food as the storm approached.The eye of the storm is expected to move inland along the coast of Baja California Sur on Monday evening, and then move inland into southern Sonora on Tuesday morning, according to NHC."Conditions will deteriorate quickly", the US weather agency warned, urging residents to seek safe shelter.Forecasters also warned of the intense storm surge the hurricane could unleash, which could be accompanied by large and destructive waves. Heavy rains could also lead to life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in areas of steep terrain.The hurricane centre said even after Polo dissipates, its remnants could produce strong gusty winds in southern New Mexico and western Texas.In Cabo San Lucas, famous for its natural rock arch, authorities restricted access to the beaches. Some restaurants also closed in the town, which acts as a base for sport fishers and whale watchers. Laura Velázquez, national coordinator of Mexico's Civil Protection Agency, said that travel will be halted in the area where the hurricane is expected to make landfall and ports will be closed.Dangerous surf and rip currents are likely along portions of the northwestern coast of Mexico and Baja California for the next day or so, meteorologists said.

schema.headline: Hurricane Polo unleashes threatening winds as it approaches Mexico

title: Iranian minister says only negotiation can end conflict after Trump rejects Hormuz deal
description: Only a "negotiated solution" can end the conflict between the US and Iran, Tehran's foreign minister has said, after President Donald Trump publicly r
body: Only a "negotiated solution" can end the conflict between the US and Iran, Tehran's foreign minister has said, after President Donald Trump publicly rejected a proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.Trump told reporters at the White House that Iran's proposal was not "acceptable" and that Tehran wanted to make a deal to open the strait to commercial shipping  within seven days because "they're losing so badly".In a post on Telegram, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi acknowledged Trump's rejection, but said Iran would wait for a "definitive" official US response.He said the president had made contradictory statements in the past.Araghchi said the conditions to open the strait were the same that had been included in a memorandum of understanding (MOU) between the US and Iran that was signed in June.Iran said it had raised reopening the strait and ending hostilities during negotiations on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York this past week.The vital waterway through which around a fifth of the world's gas and oil supply usually flows has been effectively closed since the outbreak of war in February."I'm rejecting their deal," Trump said on Saturday, adding that the US already had "total control" of the strait, with "massive amounts of oil" passing through it, causing massive rises in global oil prices and steep fuel cost increases for consumers.Araghchi wrote on Telegram that Trump "has made many good statements, as well as many contradictory ones, which unfortunately we hear frequently".He continued: "We are waiting for the mediators to convey the definitive views to us, and we will make a decision based on them."Separately, Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian, who travelled to New York for the UN general assembly, told the BBC's US news partner CBS that "distrust created by this war needs to be overcome" in order for talks to be successful. He said the Iranians were open to talks on implementing the MOU in stages in order to end the impasse, but that the "US needs to show it does not intend to overthrow our government".Pezeshkian said Trump had "tore up" the MOU when the US resumed its bombing campaign, adding: "If we don't abide by what we have written down, can we really resolve it by dialogue?"He was also asked about Iran's new Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, who was injured in the US strike which killed his father in February and has not been seen in public since. Reports have claimed he suffered serious injuries to his legs and face.Pezeshkian said he had met the supreme leader on two occasions, telling CBS he had "no specific ongoing health issues or challenges" and had been well enough to hold seven hours of talks.Oman, which has been acting as a mediator between the US and Iran, called for all parties to continue having open dialogue to resolve the crisis.Oman's foreign minister, Sayyid Badr bin Hamad bin Hamood Albusaidi, told the UN General Debate that "all parties" should cooperate with Oman in efforts to safeguard navigation in the strategic waterway.Trump's rejection of Iran's proposal was backed by US ambassador to Nato Matthew Whitaker.Speaking to Fox News on Saturday, Whitaker said that Iran had offered "half measures" and "illusory deals to make themselves look good on the world stage"."President Trump's right to reject it," he said.Meanwhile, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Saturday that economic sanctions imposed by the US were taking a toll on Iran.Posting on X, Bessent said Turkey, Oman and the United Arab Emirates had halted flights from various Iranian airlines, and some banks in the UAE and Turkey had stopped transactions with Iran.The Trump administration has dubbed an economic blockade on Iran "Operation Economic Outcast", with the White House attempting to use economic pressure to force Tehran to stop attacks on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz.But some economists have questioned whether the latest sanctions will be effective, as this depends on the reaction from Iran's major trading partners.These include China, the biggest buyer of Iranian oil, which has ignored previous US sanctions and continued to do business with Tehran.

schema.headline: Iranian minister says only negotiation can end conflict after Trump rejects Hormuz deal

title: 'Scourge' of abuse must be rooted out, says Pope during Lourdes visit
description: Pope Leo has called on French bishops to root out the "scourge" of sexual abuse in the Roman Catholic church, urging them to "maintain the greatest vi
body: Pope Leo has called on French bishops to root out the "scourge" of sexual abuse in the Roman Catholic church, urging them to "maintain the greatest vigilance".The Pope delivered the message to bishops during a private meeting at the Sanctuary of Our Holy Lady of Lourdes, a holy site in southern France, on the third day of his four-day official visit to France.A 2021 inquiry found that clergy or lay members of the Church had abused about 330,000 people as children in France over 70 years.The Pope said Mass in front of thousands of worshippers in Lourdes before later meeting survivors of abuse.The Pope told the bishops: "You have faced with determination the painful scourge of abuse of minors committed by members of the clergy or within an ecclesial context."It is important to persevere along the path you have begun, maintaining the greatest vigilance."The gathering of senior church leaders was held behind closed doors and the remarks were later released to reporters.Leo then met with seven survivors of abuse by the French clergy.The Pope "thanked them for their painful testimony and reaffirmed his commitment to ensuring that the harm they experienced is not repeated for others", the Vatican said in a statement."It was extraordinary," said survivor Jean-Marie Delbos at a news conference following the encounter with the pontiff. He said Leo listened and was informed of their cases. "I never thought I would have a Pope before me," he added.The Lourdes gathering came a day after an estimated 700,000 people flocked to the Place de la Concorde in Paris to hear the pontiff speak.Huge crowds cheered and waved as he rode down the Champs-Élysées Avenue greeting followers from his open-topped popemobile.On Friday, the Pope also met French President Emmanuel Macron.During Saturday's Mass in Paris, the Pope told worshippers that Catholics should not keep their faith to themselves but "let it overflow so that those you meet may be refreshed".The leader of the Catholic Church also addressed young people in his speech, describing them as "today's Church"."How beautiful it is to see your enthusiasm, energy and commitment, and the joy you bring to Christian communities," he said.The number of regular worshippers in France has fallen from 35% of the population in 1960 to less than 5% today, while the number of priests has shrunk by two-thirds from 25,000 in 1990 to fewer than 9,000.But in recent years there have been signs of a growing interest in religious tradition, with the number of adult baptisms more than doubling in five years to hit 10,000 in 2025.Sexual abuse inside the Catholic Church has been widespread and dates back to the 1950s.The issue was first given significant media attention in the 1980s in the US and Canada before similar stories emerged across the world, including widespread historic abuse in Ireland and the UK.Reporting by the Boston Globe newspaper in the early 2000s, dramatised in the 2015 film Spotlight, exposed widespread abuse and how paedophile priests were moved around by Church leaders instead of being held accountable. It prompted people to come forward across the US and around the world.A Church-commissioned report in 2004 said more than 4,000 US Roman Catholic priests had faced sexual abuse allegations in the last 50 years, in cases involving more than 10,000 children - mostly boys.Leo's predecessor Pope Francis tried to address the issue by holding an unprecedented summit on paedophilia in the Church, and by changing its laws to explicitly criminalise sexual abuse, but problems remain.

schema.headline: 'Scourge' of abuse must be rooted out, says Pope during Lourdes visit
